title: Joseph: They Threw Him Into a Pit to Bury the Dream—But God Was Already Writing the Ending
paragraphs: Joseph: They Threw Him Into a Pit to Bury the Dream—But God Was Already Writing the Ending

His brothers stripped him, sold him, lied about his death, and went home believing the dream was finished. Years later, they bowed before the brother they had betrayed—because what people mean for evil, God can sovereignly weave toward good.
There is a particular kind of pain that does not come from enemies.
It comes from people who know your name.
People who have eaten beside you.
People who know your weaknesses, your history, your family, your hopes.
People close enough to know exactly where betrayal will hurt.
Joseph knew that pain.

Long before he stood dressed in the authority of Egypt, long before Pharaoh placed his signet ring on Joseph's hand, long before starving nations came looking for grain, there was a teenage boy standing in front of his own brothers.
And they hated what God had shown him.

Joseph was seventeen when Genesis introduces him in the story that would define generations. He was the son Jacob loved deeply, born to Rachel, and Jacob's favoritism was painfully obvious. Genesis does not sanitize this family. Scripture does not pretend Joseph grew up in some flawless biblical household where everyone prayed together and handled conflict perfectly.
This family was complicated.
There was favoritism.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Old wounds.
Bad decisions.
And resentment growing quietly until resentment became hatred.

Jacob gave Joseph the famous garment described in Genesis 37:3. The Hebrew expression is כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים — ketonet passim. Traditionally rendered a “coat of many colors,” its precise appearance is debated; translations such as “ornate robe” or “long robe” reflect that uncertainty.
But the emotional meaning in the narrative is unmistakable.
Joseph had been singled out.
His brothers saw it.
And every time they looked at Joseph, they were reminded of their father's unequal affection.
Then Joseph dreamed.
In one dream, Joseph and his brothers were binding sheaves in a field. Joseph's sheaf stood upright, while the others gathered around and bowed to it.
His brothers immediately understood the implication.
“Are you indeed to reign over us?”
Then another dream came.
The sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed before him.
Even Jacob rebuked him.
Joseph could not yet see the road between revelation and fulfillment.
He saw the dream.
He did not see the pit.
He saw people bowing.
He did not see himself begging.
He saw elevation.
He did not see slavery.
He saw what God would eventually accomplish.
He did not see how much suffering would stand between the promise and its fulfillment.
And maybe that is where Joseph's story begins touching yours.
Because sometimes God allows you to see enough to keep walking without showing you everything walking will cost.
You thought obedience would make the road easier.
Instead, people misunderstood you.
You thought doing what was right would protect you from betrayal.
It didn't.
You prayed.
And something still collapsed.
You tried to remain faithful.
And someone else appeared to prosper while you were hurting.
Maybe you have wondered in the darkness:
“God, did I misunderstand You?”
Joseph's brothers saw him approaching from a distance one day.
Before Joseph ever reached them, they were already plotting.
Genesis 37:19 records their contempt:
בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת הַלָּזֶה בָּא — ba'al haḥalomot hallazeh ba'
Loosely and naturally:
“Here comes this dreamer.”
Then came words that expose the heart of their conspiracy:
“Come now, let us kill him…”
And then:
“we shall see what will become of his dreams.”
Think about that.
They were not merely attacking Joseph.
They believed that by destroying the dreamer, they could determine the destiny of the dream.
They stripped Joseph of his robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Genesis tells us the pit was empty and contained no water.
Then comes one of the coldest details in the entire account.
They sat down to eat.
Joseph was in the pit.
His brothers were having a meal.
Years later, Genesis 42:21 reveals something Genesis 37 does not initially emphasize: Joseph had been in distress and had pleaded with them.
Imagine hearing your own brother begging while you continue eating.
That is betrayal.
Not merely being wounded by strangers.
Being wounded by people who can hear you crying and still choose themselves.
Eventually, instead of killing Joseph, they sold him to passing traders, and Joseph was taken into Egypt.
Then the brothers dipped his robe in the blood of a goat and allowed their father to conclude that Joseph had been torn apart by a wild animal.
One lie devastated an entire household.
Jacob mourned his son.
Joseph disappeared into slavery.
And the brothers carried a secret home.
If the story ended there, Joseph would simply be another victim of human cruelty.
But Genesis contains a sentence more powerful than the pit.
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף — vayhi YHWH et-Yosef.
“And the LORD was with Joseph.”
That truth appears in Genesis 39.
Do not rush past it.
Joseph had been betrayed…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
Joseph had been sold…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
Joseph was living far from home…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
God's presence did not mean Joseph avoided suffering.
God's presence meant suffering did not have ultimate ownership of Joseph's story.
That distinction matters.
Because some believers quietly assume that if God is truly with them, nothing devastating should happen.
Joseph's life destroys that theology.
You can be loved by God and misunderstood by people.
You can walk faithfully and still be falsely accused.
You can obey God and still spend nights wondering when deliverance will come.
God's presence is not proven by the absence of trouble.
Sometimes His presence becomes most precious in the middle of it.
Joseph entered the household of Potiphar, an Egyptian official, and God caused his work to prosper. Eventually Potiphar entrusted his household to Joseph.
For a moment, perhaps life seemed to be rebuilding.
Then another scandal came.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly tried to seduce Joseph.
Joseph refused.
His response reveals the center of his integrity:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
Joseph understood something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Sin is not merely breaking a rule.
Sin is ultimately against God.
So Joseph ran.
He left his garment behind rather than leave his integrity behind.
And what did righteousness get him?
A false accusation.
Potiphar's wife used the garment Joseph abandoned while escaping to construct a lie against him.
There is almost painful irony here.
A garment had once been used by Joseph's brothers to deceive their father.
Now another garment was being used to falsely accuse Joseph.
Joseph did the right thing…
and went to prison.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You apologized and they still left.
You told the truth and people believed the lie.
You refused the compromise and lost the opportunity.
You remained faithful and watched someone dishonest move ahead.
You prayed for restoration and received another disappointment.
And somewhere inside you, perhaps you have whispered:
“What is the point of doing right if doing right still hurts?”
Joseph's story answers—not with cheap optimism, but with providence.
The prison was not proof that God had forgotten Joseph.
Genesis again emphasizes that the LORD was with him.
In prison Joseph interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. The cupbearer would be restored to his position, and Joseph asked him to remember him.
The interpretation came true.
The cupbearer was restored.
And then Scripture says he forgot Joseph.
Imagine surviving betrayal by your brothers.
Surviving slavery.
Surviving false accusation.
Then finally believing somebody might speak your name in the right room…
only to be forgotten.
Days passed.
Weeks.
Months.
Then years.
Genesis 41 tells us two full years passed before Pharaoh dreamed dreams that Egypt's wise men could not interpret.
Suddenly the cupbearer remembered.
Joseph was brought from the dungeon.
And the forgotten prisoner stood before the most powerful man in Egypt.
Pharaoh told Joseph that he had heard Joseph could interpret dreams.
Joseph could have seized the moment and marketed himself.
Instead he answered:
“It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
That is spiritual maturity forged in darkness.
The seventeen-year-old Joseph had once told people his dreams.
The older Joseph standing before Pharaoh pointed immediately to God.
Suffering had not destroyed the gift.
It had deepened the man carrying it.
Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams: seven years of extraordinary abundance would be followed by seven years of devastating famine.
Joseph then recommended wise preparation.
Pharaoh recognized unusual wisdom in him.
And in one breathtaking reversal, the prisoner became Egypt's governor.
The pit had not canceled the dream.
The prison had not canceled the dream.
The lie had not canceled the dream.
Being forgotten had not canceled the dream.
Because ultimately Joseph's future was never sitting in his brothers' hands.
And neither is God's sovereign purpose for your life sitting in the hands of the person who rejected you.
But be careful here.
Joseph's story is not a promise that every Christian who suffers will become wealthy, famous, politically powerful, or publicly vindicated.
That would distort Scripture.
The point is greater than that.
God is sovereign.
God is faithful.
God can work through circumstances human beings intended for destruction.
And sometimes His purposes are much larger than the comfort of one individual.
The famine eventually came.
Joseph's brothers traveled to Egypt looking for food.
They entered the presence of Egypt's governor without recognizing him.
And then…
they bowed.
The brothers who had mocked the dream were standing inside its fulfillment.
Can you imagine Joseph's heartbeat?
These were the faces from the pit.
The voices from the nightmare.
The men whose choices had changed the course of his life.
Now they were vulnerable before him.
Joseph possessed what wounded people often fantasize about possessing:
power over the people who hurt him.
He could punish them.
Humiliate them.
Starve them.
Make them feel helpless.
He could finally make them hurt the way he had hurt.

And the story becomes profoundly revealing because Joseph does test his brothers, particularly regarding Benjamin, and the narrative shows evidence of their changed hearts—especially when Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place.
Then Joseph can no longer contain himself.
He sends the Egyptians from the room.
And he weeps.
Not a polished little tear for religious effect.
Genesis describes such loud weeping that the Egyptians heard it.
Then Joseph says words his brothers never expected:
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine the terror.
The brother you sold is alive.
The boy you threw away has authority.
The secret you buried is standing in front of you.
Then Joseph says:
“Come near to me, please.”
Read that again.
Come near.
The men who once rejected Joseph were invited closer.
Joseph did not pretend their evil was good.
Biblical forgiveness does not require calling wickedness righteous.
Joseph explicitly acknowledges what they did.
“You sold me here.”
But he also recognizes something greater than their sin operating through history.
Later, after Jacob dies, the brothers fear Joseph may finally seek revenge.
Joseph weeps again.
And then comes the sentence that has echoed through generations.
Genesis 50:20:
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'atem ḥashavtem 'alai ra'ah; Elohim ḥashavah letovah.
A faithful rendering is:
“As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good…”
The Hebrew is striking because the verb חָשַׁב — ḥashav, carrying the sense of planning, reckoning, or intending, appears on both sides.
They intended.
God intended.
Same event.
Different intention.
Joseph does not say:
“What you did wasn't really evil.”
He calls it רָעָה — ra'ah.
Evil.
The Bible does not need to minimize human evil in order to magnify God's sovereignty.
They meant evil.
God meant good.
Not because evil magically became righteous, but because human wickedness could not overthrow divine providence.
And the “good” was bigger than Joseph receiving a promotion.
Joseph explains the purpose:
“to bring it about that many people should be kept alive.”
God was preserving lives.
God was preserving Jacob's family.
And through that family, the biblical story would continue toward Israel, Judah, David…
and ultimately Jesus Christ.
This is where Joseph's story becomes larger than Joseph.
Joseph is not Jesus, and we should not flatten the differences between them. Yet Joseph's story contains patterns that prepare Christian readers to recognize something even greater in Christ.
A beloved son rejected by his own.
Humiliated.
Handed over.
Suffering despite innocence.
Then exalted.
And through what looked like catastrophic defeat, God brought deliverance to others.
Then we reach Jesus.
Jesus was not merely a dreamer thrown into a pit.
He is the Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He was rejected.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
Human beings meant the cross as an instrument of shame, suffering, and death.
Yet God accomplished redemption through the very cross intended to destroy Him.
Peter would later proclaim concerning Jesus that He was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, while lawless men crucified and killed Him.
Human responsibility.
Divine sovereignty.
At the same cross.
Then resurrection.
What looked like the end became the announcement that death itself had been defeated.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where the story stops being safely about Joseph's brothers.
Because we like identifying with Joseph.
We like imagining ourselves as the misunderstood dreamer.
The betrayed one.
The falsely accused one.
The forgotten one who eventually gets vindicated.
But what if sometimes…
we are the brothers?
What if jealousy has lived inside us?
What if we have secretly resented someone else's blessing?
What if we smiled publicly while bitterness grew privately?
What if we damaged someone with our words?
What if we betrayed trust?
What if there are things in our past we desperately hope never walk through the door and say:
“I am Joseph”?
We do not only need a God who can rescue Joseph from a pit.
We need a Savior who can forgive Joseph's brothers.
We need Jesus.
Because the deepest scandal in Scripture is not merely that innocent people suffer.
It is that guilty people like us can be offered grace because the truly innocent Christ suffered in the place of sinners.
This is why Christianity is not self-improvement wearing a cross necklace.
The Gospel is not:
“Become impressive enough for God to accept you.”
It is that sinners who could never save themselves are called to repent and trust in Jesus Christ—the crucified and risen Lord.
Grace does not pretend your sin never mattered.
Grace says it mattered so much that Christ bore sin's judgment at the cross.
Forgiveness is not God shrugging at evil.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
And resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word.
Maybe your scandal is known.
Maybe yours is hidden.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe everybody knows what was done to you.
Maybe your pit was betrayal.
Maybe your prison has been shame.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun a chapter you cannot rewrite.
You cannot change yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem a life you thought yesterday had permanently defined.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Real grace calls us out of hiding.
Real grace produces repentance.
Real grace teaches us to confess rather than perform.
Real grace does not merely make guilty people feel better.
It begins transforming them.
That is why our theme is not “From Scandal to Pretending Nothing Happened.”
It is:
He rewrites the meaning of the chapter without pretending the chapter never happened.
Joseph still had a pit in his history.
But the pit no longer possessed his future.
The betrayal remained part of his testimony.
But betrayal did not become his identity.
His brothers' sin was real.
But their sin was not stronger than God's providence.
And your darkest chapter does not have greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been carrying hatred toward the person who threw you into your pit.
Joseph's forgiveness does not teach that abuse should be tolerated, that boundaries are sinful, that justice never matters, or that trust must instantly be restored.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical. Trust can require truth, repentance, wisdom, time, and evidence of change.
But Christian forgiveness does mean surrendering personal vengeance to God.
You cannot keep drinking bitterness and expect your soul to remain untouched.
Maybe the person you need to bring before Christ tonight is not the person who betrayed you.
Maybe it is you.
Maybe you became hard.
Maybe disappointment slowly turned into unbelief.
Maybe church hurt became an excuse to run from Jesus.
Maybe secret sin became your anesthesia.
Maybe you have been smiling online while spiritually bleeding behind the screen.
No more hiding.
Bring it to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where wisdom requires help.
Make restitution where possible.
Tell the truth.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows the chapter you are afraid to show Him.
And He is still calling sinners to Himself.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that grace still reaches people in pits.
Do not underestimate what happens when believers stop pretending.
Someone else's confession can become another person's courage.
Someone else's testimony can become another person's reason to seek Christ.
There may come a night when betrayal starts talking again.
A night when the old accusation comes back.
A night when you wonder whether God has forgotten where you are.
Come back and remember:
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף.
The LORD was with Joseph.
Let your feed become one more place where people encounter biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

It does not buy God's blessing, prove your faith, or make you more pleasing to Him—Christ alone is our righteousness. But generous support can be one genuine way to participate in spreading resources that point people toward Jesus.
And there is much more waiting for believers who are serious about growing deeper.
If this ministry has strengthened you, consider helping strengthen the person who has not discovered it yet.
Follow.
Save these words for the night you need them again.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because confession, testimony, prayer, and encouragement can turn a comment section into a place where people stop hiding.
Because somewhere tonight, another Joseph is staring at the walls of a pit.
Another betrayed believer thinks the betrayal was the ending.
Another forgotten person believes silence means God has left.
Another guilty brother is wondering whether grace could possibly still have his name on it.
And another wounded heart is about to discover the truth the enemy desperately wants buried:
What they threw into the pit was not beyond the reach of God—and what you surrender to Jesus is never beyond the reach of redemption.
